Comprehensive Guide: How to Map a D38999 Mil-Spec Pinout

Published: August 2026 • Category: Industrial & Engineering • No Sign-Up / 100% Free / No Registration

Mil-spec circular connectors appear on every aircraft, missile, ground vehicle, and naval system because they survive vibration, temperature cycling, fluids, and repeated mating cycles that commercial connectors cannot tolerate. Among them, the MIL-STD-38999 family is the workhorse, and its D38999 series of high-density connectors is where most modern pinout work happens. This guide walks through exactly how a D38999 connector is selected and how a pinout is built, ending with a clean wire list you can hand to a harness shop.

The first decision is the shell size. D38999 shell sizes run from 9 to 25, and the number reflects the overall envelope of the connector, not the pin count. A small shell like size 9 is suited to a handful of signals in a tight space, while a size 25 housing can carry over a hundred contacts. Choosing the shell means balancing the mounting hole available in your bulkhead or box, the number of circuits you must break, and the bending radius of the attached bundle. It is common to prototype the mechanical fit before committing to a part number.

Inside the shell sits the insert, defined by its arrangement number. The arrangement encodes the exact pattern and count of the contacts. The 11-35 arrangement, for example, holds thirteen size #22D contacts, while the 23-35 arrangement packs a hundred, and the 25-35 reaches 128. Because the arrangement fixes the pin count, choosing it early anchors the rest of the design. The TopWebTool mapper embeds the common arrangement catalog for shell sizes 9 through 25, so the pin count, contact size, and contact style are always consistent with the MIL-STD-38999 tables.

Contact size determines what you can terminate. D38999 inserts use standard contact sizes designated as #22D, #20, #16, and #12. A #22D contact accepts small wire, roughly AWG 22 to 28, and carries modest current, while a #16 contact accepts heavier AWG 16 to 20 wire and carries more current, and a #12 contact is for the heaviest feeders. Matching the wire gauge to the contact size is non-negotiable: crimping an AWG 16 wire into a #22D cavity produces a poor mechanical retention and a thermally overloaded contact.

Once the shell and arrangement are locked, the actual mapping begins. Every pin gets a signal name from the electrical schematic, a wire color from the MIL-STD-681 sequence, and a note for gauge or destination. The discipline at this stage is what separates a buildable wire list from a bundle of crossed wires. Signal names should be identical to the schematic net names so the harness can be traced end to end, and the wire color should be recorded per pin so the technician can verify each conductor before termination.

Wire colors deserve more attention than they usually receive. MIL-STD-681 defines the color-coding scheme used in mil-spec wiring, and the base colors are black, brown, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, gray, and white. When a bundle has more conductors than base colors, stripes and combinations extend the palette. The mapper assigns base colors in sequence to every pin automatically, which is a fast start; for a production wire list you should still verify each assignment against your program's wire identification standard.

The result of the mapping effort is the wire list. For each populated pin, the list records the pin number, signal name, wire color, and notes. This table is the single source of truth that drives wire cutting, stripping, crimping, and pin insertion on the build floor, and it doubles as the documentation for maintenance technicians later. Exporting it as a CSV file lets you import the list into your ERP, MRP, or spreadsheets without retyping a single pin.

Good pinout mapping anticipates the physical realities of the connector. Rear-view and front-view are not the same: when you look at the back of a connector, the pin numbering is mirrored compared with the mating face. Never assign signals from memory of a previous connector; always verify the view direction the drawing expects. Spare pins are normal and should be left unmapped but counted, and you should reserve a few spare contacts in the arrangement for future growth rather than populating every cavity on day one.

Validation closes the loop. After the wire list is generated, walk the connector: confirm every pin that needs a signal has one, confirm every signal exists on both ends of the harness, and spot-check the wire gauge against the contact size. A wire list that survives this walk is ready to build. The interactive mapper makes the whole workflow fast, but the engineering judgment, the view direction, the gauge matching, and the documentation discipline remain the human part of the job.

Start small and iterate. Map a single 13-pin 11-35 connector end to end, generate the CSV, and review it against the schematic. That exercise builds the muscle memory for the hundred-pin inserts that follow, and it is exactly the kind of practice the TopWebTool Mil-Spec Connector Pinout Mapper is designed to make routine.
